root.note: Venetian s-ciao from Latin sclavus is the standard account; the word spread over Italy in the 1800s and 1900s.

history: Ciao began as a very polite phrase. In Venice people used to say s-ciào vostro, ‘I am your slave’, meaning ‘at your service’. The Venetian word s-ciào comes from Latin sclavus, the same root as Italian schiavo, ‘slave’. In time the formula became shorter and friendlier, and in the 1900s ciao spread from northern Italy to the whole country and to the world. It is used for both ‘hello’ and ‘goodbye’, but only between people who say tu. With a stranger, an official or an older person you say buongiorno or buonasera, and arrivederci or arrivederLa. English borrowed ciao early in the 20th century, and Spanish and Portuguese have chao and tchau.
historyEinfach: Ciao comes from a Venetian polite phrase, ‘I am your servant’. The word is from Latin sclavus, ‘slave’. Today it means hello and goodbye. Use it with friends and family, not with officials or older strangers.

elsewhere.text: In Bavaria and Austria, servus means both ‘hello’ and ‘goodbye’. It comes from Latin servus, ‘servant’, so the idea is the same: a greeting built on ‘I am your servant’. It is a parallel, not a loan from Italian.
